notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Older black plates show a black dot in the middle; newer plates are white with a blue bar on top.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: Generation 3 uses a black car, as in Peru and Uruguay.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: Generation 4 smallcam coverage exists, as in Peru and Brazil.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Round concrete poles carrying three lines in an alternating pattern are very common; doubled-up poles are a good clue too.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Wooden poles occur with or without crossbars; wooden A-frame poles in South America are found only here.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons are white with red; no other country in the Americas uses them.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Road lines are mainly dashed white, double yellow, or a mix of the two.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Kilometre markers are white with a black strip on top giving the road number; RN means national, RP provincial.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: Yellow and red rectangular reflectors on guardrails; the neighbour to the east has them too but with a different support shape.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Most of the country is flat, treeless and sparsely populated, with a wide-open desolate feel.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Far western areas are mountainous; mountains are rare in the east.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Red soil in Misiones can look like southern Brazil.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Sandy soil with lots of low trees and bushes in Chaco and Formosa.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Reddish pavement lined with long needle-grass is common in San Luis.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Flat barren steppe with low grass and few bushes marks central-south Patagonia, down to Tierra del Fuego.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Beech forests are common in Tierra del Fuego.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Tall bunched reeds with fluffy white heads define the Pampas region.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Vineyards with mountains to the west and flat land to the east point to the outskirts of Mendoza.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Single rows of tall thin poplars on flat land are common around Neuquén.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Short fan-leaved wax palms in low-density stands, most common in Formosa.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Candelabra-shaped cardón cacti with golden-brown spines in the northwestern highlands.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Monkey puzzle trees grow in western Neuquén.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The caldén, a sinuous deciduous tree, is mostly found in La Pampa.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Sugarcane is most common in Tucumán, with pockets in Salta and Jujuy.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Most tree plantations are in Entre Ríos; Uruguay and southern Brazil have them too.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Wooden hook poles in the style of Latvia are unique to La Rioja and Mendoza.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: White vertical pole stickers with several digits are found in Tucumán.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Yellow rectangular signs with chevrons at the bottom and road numbers on top mark some T-junctions in La Pampa.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Red brick buildings like those in Bolivia occur in the northwest, especially western Jujuy.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Quartzite facades, orange tiled roofs, attached garages and vault-shaped porches around Mar del Plata.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Salt pans are typically in Jujuy; also in southwestern Bolivia and northeastern Chile.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Snowy mountains to the north are only seen from Ushuaia, the southernmost city.
